name: Grounded theory
summary: Theory is built from the data through constant comparison: code closely, raise the important codes into categories, link the categories, collect more data to test them, and stop when new material adds nothing.
notes: Choose your tradition at the start (constructivist or Straussian) and say so in your write-up; the phases below are the same, but how you treat your own interpretation differs.

Not yet built for this method: the in-vivo shortcut prompts, constant-comparison prompts when a code is applied, labeled links between categories, and the saturation chart. The phases, prompts, and checklists work now.

phases.title: Initial coding
phases.goal: Code line by line or incident by incident, using the participants' own words where you can.
memo_prompts: What is happening here? What does this person seem to be doing or facing?
exit_checklist: Wrote memos on the most puzzling incidents

phases.title: Focused coding
phases.goal: Use the most frequent and most telling codes to sort through large amounts of data.
memo_prompts: Which codes explain the most? Which ones are doing the same work under different names?
exit_checklist: Compared incidents within each focused code

phases.title: Theoretical (axial) coding
phases.goal: Relate categories to one another: conditions, actions, and consequences.
memo_prompts: How does this category relate to the others? Under what conditions?
exit_checklist: Drafted a map of the categories

phases.title: Theoretical sampling
phases.goal: Decide what to collect next in order to test and fill out the categories.
memo_prompts: What do you not know yet? Who or what could tell you?
exit_checklist: Listed the gaps in each category
Chose the next cases or sources to collect

phases.title: Saturation
phases.goal: Judge whether new material is still changing your categories, and say how you decided.
memo_prompts: What did the latest sources add that was new?
exit_checklist: Checked that recent sources raised no new categories
